main.title: Haunting Ground
main.subtitle: An escape shared with a dog
main.summary: Haunting Ground is Capcom's PlayStation 2 survival horror game, first released in Japan on 21 April 2005. Fiona Belli wakes inside an unfamiliar castle after a car accident and tries to find a way out. She frees a white shepherd named Hewie, whose help becomes essential as the inhabitants pursue her. Exploration and escape carry more weight than direct fighting. The castle's rooms offer clues, locked routes and hiding places, while the presence of another living creature gives Fiona someone to rely on in a threatening environment.

cards.heading: An escape shared with a dog
cards.text: Haunting Ground is Capcom's PlayStation 2 survival horror game, first released in Japan on 21 April 2005. Fiona Belli wakes inside an unfamiliar castle after a car accident and tries to find a way out. She frees a white shepherd named Hewie, whose help becomes essential as the inhabitants pursue her. Exploration and escape carry more weight than direct fighting. The castle's rooms offer clues, locked routes and hiding places, while the presence of another living creature gives Fiona someone to rely on in a threatening environment.

cards.heading: Trust changes what Hewie will do
cards.text: The player controls Fiona directly and gives Hewie commands. Calling him, asking him to investigate or sending him toward a pursuer can create an opening, but his cooperation depends on their relationship. Praising and caring for the dog makes that bond part of play rather than simply a story detail. Fiona's own movement consumes stamina, and exhaustion makes escape harder. A chase therefore asks for more than holding a direction: the player must judge the route, the companion's position and the resources left to keep moving.

cards.heading: Fear changes the picture
cards.text: When Fiona becomes overwhelmed, panic affects both her behaviour and the presentation, making an already dangerous pursuit more difficult to control. Hiding and using the environment can buy time, while items offer ways to recover or hinder an enemy. Director Kazuhiro Tsuchiya's team built a vulnerable protagonist whose limited means keep the emphasis on evasion. The game received a mixed critical response, with praise for its atmosphere and partnership alongside criticism of repetition. Its relationship between the pursued character and her dog remains its most recognisable idea.

main.title: Forza Motorsport
main.summary: Forza Motorsport is a 2005 simulation racing video game developed by Turn 10 Studios and published by Microsoft Game Studios for the Xbox gaming system.

cards.heading: Forza Motorsport
cards.text: Forza Motorsport brought Turn 10 Studios' driving simulation to Xbox in 2005. Published by Microsoft Game Studios, it offered more than two hundred cars, a mixture of real and fictional courses, and online racing through Xbox Live. It began the Forza series, which continued across subsequent Xbox generations. The original received widespread critical acclaim and sold more than one hundred thousand copies in North America during its release month. Its later availability through Xbox 360 backwards compatibility kept the first game accessible on the following console.

main.title: Brain Age: Train Your Brain in Minutes a Day!
main.summary: Brain Age: Train Your Brain in Minutes a Day!, known as Dr Kawashima's Brain Training: How Old Is Your Brain? in the PAL regions, is a 2005 edutainment puzzle video game by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS.

cards.text: Brain Age: Train Your Brain in Minutes a Day!, known as Dr Kawashima's Brain Training: How Old Is Your Brain? in the PAL regions, is a 2005 edutainment puzzle video game by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS. It is inspired by the work of Japanese neuroscientist Ryuta Kawashima, who appears as a caricature of himself guiding the player.

Stroop tests, arithmetic and Sudoku form part of Brain Age's short puzzle sessions. The touch screen and microphone supply the answers, making it one of Nintendo's Touch! Generations games aimed at a broad audience. It won several awards and had sold 19.01 million copies worldwide by September 30, 2015. Claims about its scientific effectiveness also prompted debate. Nintendo later brought the game to Japan's Wii U eShop in 2014.

It was followed by a sequel titled Brain Age 2: More Training in Minutes a Day!, and was later followed by two redesigns and Brain Age Express for the Nintendo DSi's DSiWare service which uses popular puzzles from these titles as well as several new puzzles, and Brain Age: Concentration Training for Nintendo 3DS. The latest installment in the series, Dr Kawashima's Brain Training for Nintendo Switch, for the Nintendo Switch, was first released in Japan on December 27, 2019.

main.title: killer7
main.subtitle: Seven personalities on predetermined paths
main.summary: Seven personalities follow predetermined routes through a political action adventure, with puzzles and combat built around their different abilities.

cards.heading: Suda and Mikami begin an unusual project
cards.text: killer 7 is Grasshopper Manufacture's 2005 action adventure, directed by Goichi Suda and released by Capcom. It combines restricted routes, changing personalities and a political story drawing on relations between Japan, the United States and neighbouring countries. Suda recalled Shinji Mikami inviting him to make a GameCube project for an international audience. That brief gave the team the opportunity to develop an unfamiliar form of action game.

cards.heading: Colour carries the image
cards.text: Discussing the later PC version, Suda explains that killer7 relied heavily on colour shading rather than many textures. Its flat regions and sharp silhouettes could therefore remain legible at a higher resolution. He also distinguishes Grasshopper's original GameCube production from the PlayStation 2 version handled elsewhere, explaining why the former mattered as the port's basis. Version history is part of the image's history here. The same title can reach new hardware through work that preserves some presentation choices while changing how they are displayed.

cards.heading: Sound can break the spell
cards.text: Sound director Masafumi Takada describes repeatedly adjusting killer7's audio while playing it, asking the programmer to implement changes and omitting sounds he did not need. When he wanted discomfort, he deliberately shifted effects slightly away from their expected pitch. He also describes lowering audio before a surprise so the next change could register more strongly. The soundtrack is therefore doing more than maintaining a mood. It can draw the listener into a place, interrupt that comfort, then make the return to a calmer passage felt.

cards.heading: A route chosen at each intersection
cards.text: Capcom released killer 7 in Japan on June 9, 2005. Predetermined routes concentrate movement into a choice of direction, with intersections offering different paths. The limited movement gives framing and timing particular importance. Its high-contrast images, changing personalities and deliberately opaque political story make the game immediately distinctive.

cards.heading: Paths, puzzles and changing personalities
cards.text: The player controls the on-screen character, a member of the killer7 group, from a third-person view using the gamepad. The gameplay consists of elements of first-person shooter and action-adventure game with restricted movement (i.e. "on rails")—rather than allowing free motion, the game limits the on-screen character to predetermined paths through the environment. The on-screen character moves forward by holding a button and reverses direction with another button press. At intersections, the player may choose which path to take. Progress is made by navigating the environment and solving puzzles. Some puzzles require the talents of a specific killer7 member. The player may switch between available members via a menu in the pause screen at any time; not all personalities may be awake at a start of a mission, and requires defeating a number of enemies before they can be awakened. Other puzzles require magical rings or other items collected throughout the game.

cards.heading: Blood supplies abilities and upgrades
cards.text: Defeated Smiles yield "thick blood" and "thin blood". Thin blood is used to recover the characters' stamina and fuel special abilities. Thick blood functions similarly to experience points, and players gain more by shooting Smiles' critical points. The player may redeem thick blood for "serum" while in "Harman's Room", checkpoints that appear throughout the game. Serum is used to improve the attributes of the characters such as "power" and "speed". This also unlocks special abilities for the characters. Players may save their game in designated Harman's Rooms.

cards.heading: A high-contrast style divides reviewers
cards.text: Killer7 received divided reviews and sparked debates about depictions of sex and violence in video games and the status of video games as art. James Mielke of 1UP.com likened the game's high-contrast art style to noir and neo-noir film such as Se7en. He found that despite poor pacing and stilted gameplay, the "quirky scripting and edgy plot" were strong draws, and called Killer7 one of the "most artfully designed footnotes in gaming history". Edge magazine's reviewers echoed this sentiment and predicted that the game would "[pave the way] for future creative leeway", crediting the director with an unwavering artistic vision. Eurogamer's Kristan Reed was keenly aware of the game's limited appeal, calling it "a concept game, an arthouse game, a simple game, an often beautiful game, but most certainly never an everyman's game".

main.title: Trauma Center: Under the Knife
main.subtitle: A surgeon takes the touchscreen
main.summary: Trauma Center: Under the Knife is Atlus' Nintendo DS medical thriller combining stylus-controlled operations with a story about young surgeon Derek Stiles. A new artificial disease called GUILT brings him into the work of the organisation Caduceus, while his unusual Healing Touch provides an exceptional ability under pressure. Story scenes introduce the people and the next medical emergency before the player moves to the operating table. The handheld's touchscreen becomes the working surface, turning a list of instruments into a set of precise actions that must keep a patient alive.

cards.heading: A surgeon takes the touchscreen
cards.text: Trauma Center: Under the Knife is Atlus' Nintendo DS medical thriller combining stylus-controlled operations with a story about young surgeon Derek Stiles. A new artificial disease called GUILT brings him into the work of the organisation Caduceus, while his unusual Healing Touch provides an exceptional ability under pressure. Story scenes introduce the people and the next medical emergency before the player moves to the operating table. The handheld's touchscreen becomes the working surface, turning a list of instruments into a set of precise actions that must keep a patient alive.

cards.heading: Choose the instrument and make the movement
cards.text: Operations take place from above the affected area, with tool icons arranged around the touchscreen. The stylus makes incisions, removes objects, closes wounds and performs other procedures appropriate to the instrument selected. A time limit and the patient's vital signs keep the sequence under pressure. Reading the briefing and following instructions help establish what needs to be treated, but recognising the next action quickly becomes essential once several problems compete for attention. Accuracy matters because a careless movement can make the patient's condition harder to stabilise.

cards.heading: A hospital drama changes the scale of a gesture
cards.text: Conversations and portraits connect the operations with Derek's colleagues and his responsibilities as a doctor. The science-fiction threat then pushes the procedures beyond familiar injuries, turning some encounters with GUILT into elaborate medical confrontations. The Healing Touch provides a special response when the ordinary pace becomes overwhelming. The combination gives the touchscreen actions a clear dramatic purpose: selecting an instrument is part of an attempt to save a particular person. A successful operation resolves both a demanding sequence of movements and the immediate crisis established by the story.

main.title: Conker: Live & Reloaded
main.subtitle: Conker returns with a new coat of fur
main.summary: Conker: Live & Reloaded is Rare's Xbox remake of Conker's Bad Fur Day, released in North America on 21 June 2005. The single-player adventure revisits the squirrel's increasingly unpleasant journey with extensively rebuilt visuals and a small number of changes to enemies and equipment. Its mixture of platforming, film parody and adult comedy remains at the centre. Alongside that familiar campaign, Rare created a substantially different multiplayer game for Xbox Live, making the release both a return to the Nintendo 64 adventure and a new experiment in team-based console combat.

cards.heading: Conker returns with a new coat of fur
cards.text: Conker: Live & Reloaded is Rare's Xbox remake of Conker's Bad Fur Day, released in North America on 21 June 2005. The single-player adventure revisits the squirrel's increasingly unpleasant journey with extensively rebuilt visuals and a small number of changes to enemies and equipment. Its mixture of platforming, film parody and adult comedy remains at the centre. Alongside that familiar campaign, Rare created a substantially different multiplayer game for Xbox Live, making the release both a return to the Nintendo 64 adventure and a new experiment in team-based console combat.

cards.heading: A class determines how a soldier helps the team
cards.text: Multiplayer places the SHC against the Tediz, with six soldier classes offering distinct weapons, strengths and weaknesses. A sniper's range, a Sneeker's infiltration tools and a heavier soldier's durability encourage different contributions to the same objective. Terminals dispense equipment and vehicles, while upgrade orbs expand a character's capabilities until death returns the orb to the battlefield. The player has to consider what the team currently needs as well as the immediate target. Choosing a class changes which route, opponent or piece of equipment is most useful to pursue.

cards.heading: Two different uses for a familiar cast
cards.text: Rare began developing the Xbox version after Microsoft's acquisition of the studio in 2002. Robin Beanland's music and the campaign's familiar characters connect it to the earlier release, while the class-based multiplayer gives the same world a new structure. Vehicles, equipment terminals and team objectives create a broader battlefield than the original multiplayer arenas. The two halves offer distinct reasons to return: one revisits Conker's comic adventure in a more detailed presentation, while the other places his world inside the online team-play ambitions of the original Xbox era.

main.title: Battlefield 2
main.summary: Battlefield 2 is a 2005 first-person shooter game developed by Digital Illusions CE and published by Electronic Arts for Microsoft Windows.

cards.heading: Modern warfare on Windows
cards.text: Battlefield 2 is a 2005 first-person shooter game developed by Digital Illusions CE and published by Electronic Arts for Microsoft Windows. It is the third installment in the Battlefield series. It was released on June 21, 2005, in North America.

cards.heading: Squads under a commander
cards.text: Battlefield 2 places infantry and vehicles on a modern battlefield. Players use contemporary weapons and can organise into squads under a commander, giving teamwork a structure across the map. The single-player missions stage clashes between US Marines, China and the fictional Middle Eastern Coalition. Multiplayer makes coordinating these different roles part of the contest, with squads pursuing their immediate objectives within the wider battle.

cards.heading: Reception and community servers
cards.text: The game received critical acclaim and, like its predecessor, is considered one of the greatest games of all time. On June 30, 2014, the multiplayer master server was shut down alongside other GameSpy-powered titles, although it can still be played online through fan-created mods with alternative servers. In 2017, Electronic Arts demanded the takedown of modified versions of Battlefield 2 on alternative servers distributed by a group known as "Revive Network", alleging copyright infringement.

main.title: Advance Wars: Dual Strike
main.subtitle: Another front opens
main.summary: Advance Wars: Dual Strike is Intelligent Systems' turn-based strategy game for Nintendo DS. The Allied Nations confront Black Hole in Omega Land, where the enemy is draining energy from the landscape. Armies of infantry, tanks, aircraft and ships contest a grid of properties and terrain. Captured factories supply reinforcements, while headquarters offer a direct target. The colourful presentation makes each unit easy to distinguish, but the campaign still asks the player to balance local victories against the money and positions needed for the next turn.

cards.heading: Another front opens
cards.text: Advance Wars: Dual Strike is Intelligent Systems' turn-based strategy game for Nintendo DS. The Allied Nations confront Black Hole in Omega Land, where the enemy is draining energy from the landscape. Armies of infantry, tanks, aircraft and ships contest a grid of properties and terrain. Captured factories supply reinforcements, while headquarters offer a direct target. The colourful presentation makes each unit easy to distinguish, but the campaign still asks the player to balance local victories against the money and positions needed for the next turn.

cards.heading: Two commanders, one army
cards.text: An army can be assigned two commanding officers, with the player switching between their different strengths. CO powers alter the conditions of a turn, while a Tag Power allows both commanders to use their Super CO powers in succession. That can give one army a devastating period of uninterrupted action. Preparing the opportunity matters as much as activating it: units need to be close enough to exploit the advantage. The additional commander changes planning before the special move rather than merely supplying another attack animation.

cards.heading: Keeping both battles in view
cards.text: The DS allows selected missions to split the conflict between two fronts. Attention can move from the main battlefield to another engagement above it, while maps and unit information make use of the extra screen elsewhere. Weather, fog of war and terrain continue to affect how safely a force can advance. The second display extends an established strategy language instead of replacing it. A player who recognises the old units still has to learn how activity on one part of the operation can support another.

main.title: Steambot Chronicles
main.subtitle: A walking machine in an ordinary working world
main.summary: Steambot Chronicles is Irem's PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in Japan on 30 June 2005. It imagines an industrial age where Trotmobiles, walking machines used for transport and labour, have become part of daily life. The player can travel, take jobs, customise a machine and become involved with musicians and other inhabitants. The adventure leaves room between its central events for those smaller activities. A machine that can fight is also a vehicle for finding work and reaching the next place, giving the world a practical, lived-in character.

cards.heading: A walking machine in an ordinary working world
cards.text: Steambot Chronicles is Irem's PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in Japan on 30 June 2005. It imagines an industrial age where Trotmobiles, walking machines used for transport and labour, have become part of daily life. The player can travel, take jobs, customise a machine and become involved with musicians and other inhabitants. The adventure leaves room between its central events for those smaller activities. A machine that can fight is also a vehicle for finding work and reaching the next place, giving the world a practical, lived-in character.

cards.heading: Let the journey become something else
cards.text: Different activities use different parts of the game's systems. Performing music becomes a rhythm game, mechanical adjustments change a Trotmobile and trading connects travel to the local economy. The player moves between them rather than remaining inside one uninterrupted combat campaign. These choices give a visit to town several possible purposes: earn money, meet someone or prepare for another journey. The sandbox structure allows the character's life to gather around the larger plot, making an apparently small detour part of the way the player comes to know the setting.

cards.heading: An open-ended idea with a short series
cards.text: Kazuma Kujo produced the game for Irem. North American publisher Atlus released it in 2006, with 505 Games handling PAL territories later that year. A larger sequel was announced and shown in 2006 but eventually cancelled in 2011, leaving the original as the fullest expression of this particular world. Smaller related games explored other parts of the concept. Steambot Chronicles remains distinctive for allowing the same machine to belong to work, travel and adventure, while music and everyday transactions give the player reasons to spend time outside a battle.

main.title: We Love Katamari
main.subtitle: The fans ask for another roll
main.summary: We Love Katamari is Namco's PlayStation 2 action-puzzle sequel, first released in Japan on 7 July 2005. The King of All Cosmos now receives requests from admirers of the previous game, sending the Prince out with his adhesive katamari to satisfy them. Rolling over objects makes the ball grow until things that once blocked its path become part of it. The sequel keeps that simple action while changing what each assignment asks the player to collect, where to roll and how success is measured.

cards.heading: The fans ask for another roll
cards.text: We Love Katamari is Namco's PlayStation 2 action-puzzle sequel, first released in Japan on 7 July 2005. The King of All Cosmos now receives requests from admirers of the previous game, sending the Prince out with his adhesive katamari to satisfy them. Rolling over objects makes the ball grow until things that once blocked its path become part of it. The sequel keeps that simple action while changing what each assignment asks the player to collect, where to roll and how success is measured.

cards.heading: A familiar action with new conditions
cards.text: Different requests reshape the same rolling controls. An objective may emphasise a certain kind of object or put the Prince in surroundings that change the route through a stage. Size remains the basic language: a small ball squeezes between familiar household things, while a larger one absorbs parts of the environment that seemed fixed moments earlier. The player learns each place by the order in which it becomes collectible. These changes give individual tasks a character without requiring a different set of controls for every challenge.

cards.heading: A sequel about making a sequel
cards.text: Keita Takahashi returned to direct after initially resisting another Katamari game. The fans appearing inside it turn that real pressure for more into part of the fiction. Multiplayer includes both competition and cooperative rolling, asking two people to coordinate the movement of one ball. A varied soundtrack again accompanies the shifts in scale and setting. The 2023 Reroll+ Royal Reverie remaster brought the adventure to later platforms, while the original remains the second Katamari game and the last in the series directed by Takahashi.
